title: I Almost Ruined My Favorite Pot: How to Clean Burnt Pots with $1 Pantry Staples
description: Stop scrubbing! Learn how to clean burnt pots using baking soda and vinegar. Save $40 on new cookware with this $0.30 frugal Aldi pantry hack.
story: Last Tuesday, I was trying to meal prep a massive pot of chili using a $5 bag of dry beans from Aldi. I got caught up responding to emails and—poof—the bottom of my pot was a blackened, crusty mess. Replacing a decent stainless steel pot can cost $50 at Target, and I wasn't about to blow my weekly grocery budget on a mistake. I've learned the hard way that scrubbing with steel wool just ruins the finish. The first time I tested this hack, I didn't use enough vinegar and the stains wouldn't budge—make sure you get that acidic ratio right! This method is a total lifesaver for my tiny apartment kitchen because it uses stuff I already have under the sink. It's way cheaper than buying specialized cleaners like Bar Keepers Friend, though I love that stuff too. This cost me maybe 30 cents in supplies and saved me from a literal workout at the sink.
ingredients: 1 cup distilled white vinegar (Heinz or store brand)
1 cup tap water (or enough to cover the burnt area)
instructions: Step 1: Pour the water and white vinegar into the burnt pot and place it on the stove over medium heat until it reaches a simmer.
Step 2: Once it's bubbling, remove the pot from the heat and stir in the baking soda—it will fizz up like a middle school science project, which is exactly what you want.
Step 3: Let the pot sit and cool for about 15 minutes; you’ll see the black scorched bits starting to flake off and float to the top.
Step 4: Empty the pot and give it a quick wipe with a sponge and a little Dawn soap; the burnt layer should slide right off into the sink.
proHack: If you have a really stubborn carbon layer, don't just soak it in cold water. Re-heat the vinegar and water mixture until it's almost boiling before adding the soda; the heat helps the chemical reaction penetrate the burnt sugars much faster.
storage: Keep your gallon of vinegar in a cool, dark place under the sink. If you have leftover baking soda in the box, keep it sealed in a plastic bag so it doesn't absorb 'fridge smells' and lose its cleaning punch.

faqs.question: Can I use apple cider vinegar instead?
faqs.answer: You can, but it's more expensive. Plain white vinegar is more acidic and cheaper, making it the better frugal choice for cleaning.

faqs.question: How do I prevent the vinegar smell from taking over my apartment?
faqs.answer: Turn on your stove vent fan or crack a window before you start simmering; the smell dissipates quickly once the pot is rinsed.
